'''''Cyperus esculentus''''' (also called '''chufa''',<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.seedworldusa.com/pages/chufa-info|title=Chufa Information |website=Seed World |access-date=2020-04-29}}</ref> '''tiger nut''',<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.npr.org/sections/thesalt/2016/04/27/472581773/loathed-by-farmers-loved-by-ancients-the-strange-history-of-tiger-nuts |title=Loathed By Farmers, Loved By Ancients: The Strange History of Tiger Nuts |last=Chen |first=Angus |publisher=[[NPR]] |date=April 27, 2016 |access-date=January 5, 2021}}</ref> '''atadwe''',<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ghanastar.com/lifestyle/is-atadwe-tiger-nuts-good-for-you-health-benefits-of-tiger-nuts/|title=Is Atadwe (Tiger Nuts) Good for You? Health Benefits of Tiger Nuts|date=2015-11-15|website=GhanaStar|language=en-US|access-date=2020-04-29}}</ref> '''yellow nutsedge''',<ref>{{cite web |url=https://extension.umd.edu/hgic/topics/yellow-nutsedge |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181103134941/http://extension.umd.edu/hgic/topics/yellow-nutsedge |archive-date=November 3, 2018 |title=Yellow nutsedge |website=[[University of Maryland]] Extension |access-date=January 5, 2021 }}</ref> '''earth almond''', and in [[Shona language|Chishona]], '''pfende'''<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://chestofbooks.com/food/ingredients/Guide-For-Nut-Cookery/Chufa-Earth-Almond.html |title=Chufa (Earth Almond) |website=Chest of Books |access-date=January 5, 2021}}</ref>) is a species of plant in the [[Cyperaceae|sedge family]] widespread across much of the world.<ref>{{Cite journal| doi = 10.1111/j.1541-4337.2012.00190.x| issn = 1541-4337| volume = 11| issue = 4| pages = 366–377| last1 = Sánchez-Zapata| first1 = Elena| last2 = Fernández-López| first2 = Juana| last3 = Pérez-Alvarez| first3 = José Angel| title = Tiger Nut (Cyperus esculentus) Commercialization: Health Aspects, Composition, Properties, and Food Applications| journal = [[Comprehensive Reviews in Food Science and Food Safety]]| date = 2012-07-01}}</ref> It is found in most of the Eastern Hemisphere, including [[Southern Europe]], [[Africa]] and [[Madagascar]], as well as the [[Middle East]] and the [[Indian subcontinent]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://apps.kew.org/wcsp/namedetail.do?name_id=236532 |title=World Checklist of Selected Plant Families: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew |website=[[Kew Science]] |access-date=January 5, 2021 |archive-date=April 5, 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110405084056/http://apps.kew.org/wcsp/namedetail.do?name_id=236532 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|author=John T. Kartesz|author-link=species:John T. Kartesz|url=http://bonap.net/MapGallery/County/Cyperus%20esculentus.png|title=2013 county distribution map|website=Biota of North America Program Taxonomic Data Center. |location=[[ University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill|Chapel Hill, N.C.]] |access-date=2014-07-24|archive-date=2014-08-08|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140808235741/http://bonap.net/MapGallery/County/Cyperus%20esculentus.png|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>[http://luirig.altervista.org/flora/taxa/index1.php?scientific-name=cyperus+esculentus Altervista Flora Italiana, Zigolo dolce, Yellow Nutsedge, ''Cyperus esculentus'' L. ] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140721195406/http://luirig.altervista.org/flora/taxa/index1.php?scientific-name=cyperus+esculentus |date=2014-07-21 }} includes photographs plus distribution maps for Europe and North America</ref> ''C. esculentus'' is cultivated for its edible [[tuber]]s, called earth almonds or tiger nuts (due to the stripes on their tubers and their hard shell), as a [[snack food]] and for the preparation of ''[[horchata|horchata de chufa]]'', a sweet, milk-like beverage.<ref name=cabi/><ref>{{Cite web|last=Nazish|first=Noma|title=What Are Tiger Nuts And Why Should You Eat Them?|url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/nomanazish/2018/09/22/what-are-tiger-nuts-and-why-you-should-eat-them/|access-date=2022-01-17|website=Forbes|language=en}}</ref>

''Cyperus esculentus'' can be found wild, as a weed, or as a crop. It is an [[invasive species]] outside its native range, and is readily transported accidentally to become invasive. In many countries, ''C. esculentus'' is considered a weed.<ref name="cabi">{{cite web |title=''Cyperus esculentus'' (yellow nutsedge) |url=https://www.cabi.org/isc/datasheet/17496 |publisher=CABI |access-date=31 October 2019 |date=19 November 2018 |archive-date=2 May 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190502123815/https://www.cabi.org/isc/datasheet/17496 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name=tiger>{{cite journal | last1 = Sánchez-Zapata | first1 = E | last2 = Fernández-López | first2 = J | last3 = Angel Pérez-Alvarez | first3 = J | year = 2012 | title = Tiger Nut (''Cyperus esculentus'') Commercialization: Health Aspects, Composition, Properties, and Food Applications | journal = Comprehensive Reviews in Food Science and Food Safety | volume = 11 | issue = 4| pages = 366–77 | doi=10.1111/j.1541-4337.2012.00190.x}}</ref> It is often found in wet soils such as rice paddies and peanut farms as well as well-irrigated lawns and golf courses during warm weather.

==Description==
[[Image:Chufa.jpg|thumb|right|Young plant with tuber]]
''Cyperus esculentus'' is an [[annual plant|annual]] or [[perennial]] plant, growing to {{convert|90|cm|ft|abbr=off|frac=4}} tall, with solitary stems growing from a tuber. The plant is reproduced by seeds, creeping rhizomes, and tubers.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|title=Yellow Nut Sedge: A Menace in the Corn Belt (No. 1642)|last=Stoller|first=E.W.|publisher=US Department of Agriculture, Agricultural Research Service.|year=1981}}</ref> Due to its [[cloning|clonal]] nature, ''C. esculentus'' can take advantage of soil disturbances caused by anthropogenic or natural forces.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Renne|first1=Ian J.|last2=Tracy|first2=Benjamin F.|date=2006-08-30|title=Disturbance persistence in managed grasslands: shifts in aboveground community structure and the weed seed bank|journal=Plant Ecology |language=en|volume=190|issue=1|pages=71–80|doi=10.1007/s11258-006-9191-7|s2cid=45148808|issn=1385-0237}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Oldfield |first1=Callie A.|last2=Evans|first2=Jonathan P.|date=2016-03-01|title=Twelve years of repeated wild hog activity promotes population maintenance of an invasive clonal plant in a coastal dune ecosystem|journal=Ecology and Evolution|language=en|pages=2569–2578 |doi=10.1002/ece3.2045 |pmid=27110354|pmc=4834338|issn=2045-7758|volume=6|issue=8 |doi-access=free }}</ref> The stems are triangular in section and bear slender [[leaf|leaves]] {{convert|3|–|10|mm|abbr=off|in|frac=8}} wide. The spikelets of the plant are distinctive, with a cluster of flat, oval seeds surrounded by four hanging, leaf-like [[bract]]s positioned 90 degrees from each other. They are {{convert|5|to|30|mm|abbr=on|in|frac=8}} long and linear to narrowly elliptic with pointed tips and 8 to 35 florets. The color varies from straw-colored to gold-brown. They can produce up to 2420 seeds per plant. The plant foliage is very tough and fibrous and is often mistaken for a [[Poaceae|grass]]. The roots are an extensive and complex system of fine, fibrous roots and scaly rhizomes with small, hard, spherical tubers and basal [[bulbs]] attached.

The tubers are {{convert|0.3|–|2.5|cm|in|frac=8|abbr=on}} in diameter and the colors vary between yellow, brown, and black.<ref name=Factsheet>^ USGS Weeds in the West project: Status of introduced Plants in Southern Arizona Parks, Factsheets for Cyperus esculentus L., 2003, Tucson, Arizona</ref><ref>{{Cite book |title=The Complete Guide to Edible Wild Plants |publisher=[[Skyhorse Publishing]] |others=[[United States Department of the Army]] |year=2009 |isbn=978-1-60239-692-0 |location=New York |page=43 |language=en-US |oclc=277203364 }}</ref> One plant can produce several hundred to several thousand tubers during a single growing season. With cool temperatures, the foliage, roots, rhizomes, and basal bulbs die, but the tubers survive and resprout the following spring when soil temperatures remain above {{convert|6|°C|°F|abbr=on}}.<ref name=":0" /> They can resprout up to several years later.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Stoller|first1=E. W.|last2=Wax|first2=L. M.|date=1973-01-01|title=Yellow Nutsedge Shoot Emergence and Tuber Longevity|jstor=4042258|journal=Weed Science|volume=21|issue=1|pages=76–81|doi=10.1017/S004317450003174X|s2cid=83193492 }}</ref> When the tubers germinate, many rhizomes are initiated and end in a basal bulb near the soil surface. These basal bulbs initiate the stems and leaves above ground, and fibrous roots underground. ''C. esculentus'' is wind pollinated and requires [[cross pollination]] as it is self–incompatible.

=== Similar species ===
* [[Sedges]] (''Cyperus'') have grass-like leaves and resemble each other in the appearance. They can mainly be distinguished from grasses by their triangular stems.
* Purple nutsedge (''[[Cyperus rotundus|C. rotundus]]'') is another weedy sedge that is similar to the yellow nutsedge (''C. esculentus''). These two sedges are difficult to distinguish from each other and can be found growing on the same site. Some differences are the purple spikelets and the tubers formed by ''C. rotundus'' are often multiple instead of just one at the tip. In addition the tubers have a bitter taste instead of the mild almond-like flavour of ''C. esculentus''.<ref name="Factsheet" />

==Ecology==
''Cyperus esculentus'' is a highly invasive species in [[Oceania]], [[Mexico]], some regions of the [[United States]] (where it is native{{r|castro2015}}), and the [[Caribbean]], mainly by seed dispersion.<ref name="cabi" /> It is readily transported internationally, and is adaptable to {{nowrap|re-establish}} in varied climate and soil environments.<ref name="cabi" /> In [[Japan]], it is an exotic clonal weed favorable to establish in wet habitats.<ref name="cabi" /> ''Cyperus esculentus'' serves as a larval host for ''[[Euphyes vestris]]'' (dun skipper)<ref>{{cite web |title=''Cyperus esculentus'' |url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/cyperus-esculentus/ |website=plants.ces.ncsu.edu |access-date=19 December 2023}}</ref>
and ''[[Diploschizia impigritella]]'' (yellow nut-sedge moth) in North America.<ref>{{cite web |title=Yellow Nutsedge Moth |url=https://www.butterfliesandmoths.org/species/Diploschizia-impigritella |website=www.butterfliesandmoths.org |access-date=22 January 2024}}</ref> ''Cyperus esculentus'' likely reached the [[New World]] through ocean currents before the [[Holocene]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=De Castro |first1=Olga |last2=Gargiulo |first2=Roberta |last3=Del Guacchio |first3=Emanuele |last4=Caputo |first4=Paolo |last5=De Luca |first5=Paolo |title=A molecular survey concerning the origin of ''Cyperus esculentus'' (Cyperaceae, Poales): two sides of the same coin (weed vs. crop) |url=https://academic.oup.com/aob/article/115/5/733/217532 |journal=Annals of Botany |volume=115 |pages=733–745 |issue=5 |date=2015 |doi=10.1093/aob/mcv001 |pmid=25694438 |access-date=22 January 2024}}</ref>

==Cultivation==
''Cyperus esculentus'' is cultivated in [[Egypt]], [[Spain]], [[Nigeria]], the [[United States]], [[Guatemala]], [[Mexico]], [[Chile]], [[Brazil]], [[Lebanon]], [[Syria]], [[Jordan]], [[Saudi Arabia]], [[Oman]], [[Iran]], [[Iraq]], [[Pakistan]], [[India]], [[Yemen]], [[Morocco]], [[Ivory Coast]], [[Sudan]], [[South Sudan]], [[Gambia]], [[Guinea Bissau]], [[Ghana]], [[Niger]], [[Burkina Faso]], [[Togo]], [[Benin]], [[Cameroon]], and [[Mali]], where they are used primarily as animal feed or as a side dish, but in [[Ibero-America|Hispanic]] countries they are used mainly to make [[horchata]], a sweet, milk-like beverage.[[File:Procés de cultiu de la xufa.jpeg|thumb|250px|Cultivation and growing of the ''xufa'' in the [[Valencian Community]], file by the [[Valencian Museum of Ethnology]]]]

===Climate requirements===
''Cyperus esculentus'' cultivation requires a mild climate. Low temperature, shade, and light intensity can inhibit flowering.<ref name=Factsheet/> Tuber initiation is inhibited by high levels of nitrogen, long photoperiods, and high levels of [[gibberellic acid]]. Flower initiation occurs under photoperiods of 12 to 14 hours per day.

===Soil requirements===
Tubers can develop in soil depths around 30 cm, but most occur in the top or upper part. They tolerate many adverse soil conditions including periods of drought and flooding and survive soil temperatures around {{convert|-5|°C|°F|abbr=on}}. They grow best on sandy, moist soils at a pH between 5.0 – 7.5.<ref name=Factsheet/> The densest populations of ''C. esculentus'' are often found in low-lying wetlands.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Ross|first1=Merrill A.|last2=Lembi|first2=Carole A.|title=Applied Weed Science|publisher=Prentice Hall|edition=3|year=2008|page=322|isbn=978-0-13-502814-8}}</ref> They do not tolerate salinity.<ref name=Factsheet/>

===Cultivation process===
''Cyperus esculentus'' is normally planted on previously tilled flat soils with ridges to facilitate irrigation. Seeds are planted manually on these ridges, which are approximately {{convert|60|cm|ft|abbr=on|frac=2}} apart. Distances between seeds may vary from {{convert|15|to|20|cm|in|round=0.5|abbr=on}} and seeding depth is around {{convert|8|cm|in|frac=2|abbr=on}}. A typical seeding rate for chufa is about 120 kg of tubers/ha (107 lbs/acre).<ref>N. Pascual-Seva, et al., ''Furrow-irrigated chufa crops in Valencia (Spain)'' Spanish Journal of Agricultural Research 2013 11(1), 258-267.  http://revistas.inia.es/index.php/sjar/article/view/3385/1803</ref>

They are planted between April and May and must be irrigated every week until they are harvested in November and December. Tubers develop about 6–8 weeks after seedling emergence and grow quickly during July and August. The maturing is around 90–110 days. The average yield can approach between 10 and 19 t/ha.<ref>Pascual-Seva, N., San Bautista, A., López Galarza, S., Maroto, J.V. and Pascual, B. 2012. Yield and Irrigation Water Use Efficiency for Ridge - and Bed - cultivated Chufa (''Cyperus Esculentus'' L. var. ''Sativus Boeck''). Acta Hort. (ISHS) 936:125-132</ref><ref>Reid WS, Hergert GB, Fagan WE, 1972. Development of a Prototype mechanical Harvester for Chufa (''Cyperus esculentus'' L. var ''sativus Boek''). Canadian Agricultural Engineering 14.</ref>

=== Compatibility with other crops ===
[[File:Cyperus esculentus NRCS-1.jpg|thumb|160px|The seed head of a ''Cyperus esculentus'' plant]]
''Cyperus esculentus'' is extremely difficult to remove completely once established. This is due to the plant having a stratified and layered root system, with tubers and roots being interconnected to a depth of 36 cm or more.<ref name="Factsheet" /> The tubers are connected by fragile roots that are prone to snapping when pulled, making the root system difficult to remove intact. Intermediate rhizomes can reach a length of 60 cm. The plant can quickly regenerate if a single tuber is left in place. By competing for light, water and nutrients it can reduce the vigour of neighbouring plants. It can develop into a dense colony. Patch boundaries can increase by more than one meter per year. Tubers and seed disperse with agricultural activities, soil movement or by water and wind. They are often known as a contaminant in crop seeds. When plants are small they are hard to distinguish from other weeds such as ''[[Dactylis glomerata]]'' and ''[[Elytrigia repens]]''. Thus it is hard to discover in an early stage and therefore hard to counteract. Once it is detected, mechanical removal, hand removal, grazing, damping, and herbicides can be used to inhibit ''C. esculentus''.

===Harvest and drying process===
[[File:Cyperus esculentus (Museu Valencià d'Etnologia).jpg|thumb]]
Harvest usually occurs in November or December and the leaves are scorched during the harvest. With a combine harvester, the tiger nut is pulled out of the ground. Immediately after harvesting, the tiger nuts are washed with water in order to remove sand and small stones. The drying occurs usually in the sun and can take up to three months.<ref name=month>Tigernuts Traders, S.L., ''Tigernuts Oil'', 2012, http://www.tigernut.com</ref> The temperatures and humidity levels have to be monitored very carefully during this period. The tiger nuts have to be turned every day to ensure uniform drying. The drying process ensures a longer shelf life. This prevents rot or other bacterial infections, securing quality and high nutrition levels.
Disadvantages in the drying process are shrinkage, skin wrinkles and hard nut texture.{{citation needed|date=November 2019}}

===Storage===
Tiger nut loses a considerable amount of water during drying and storage. The starch content of the tiger nut tubers decreases and the reducing sugar (invert sugar) content increases during storage.<ref>{{cite journal|title= Physical and chemical properties of chufa (''Cyperus esculentus'' L) tubers grown in the Çukurova region of Turkey |doi=10.1002/jsfa.1091 | volume=82 |issue= 6|journal=Journal of the Science of Food and Agriculture |pages=625–631|year= 2002|last1= Coşkuner|first1= Yalçın|last2= Ercan|first2= Recai|last3= Karababa|first3= Erşan|last4= Nazlıcan|first4= Ahmet Nedim}}</ref> Tiger nut can be stored dry and rehydrated by soaking without losing the crisp texture. Soaking is often done overnight. Dried tiger nuts have a hard texture and soaking is required to render them more easily edible and to ensure acceptable sensory quality.<ref name=Factsheet/>

According to the ''Consejo Regulador de Chufa de Valencia'' (Regulating Council for Valencia's Tiger Nuts),<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.chufadevalencia.org/ |title=''Consejo Regulador de Chufa de Valencia'' |publisher=Chufadevalencia.org |date=2002-12-31 |access-date=2012-06-05 |archive-date=2018-09-29 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180929104937/http://www.chufadevalencia.org/ |url-status=live }}</ref> the nutritional composition/100 ml of the Spanish beverage horchata de chufas is as follows: energy content around 66 kcal, [[protein]]s around 0.5 g, [[carbohydrate]]s over 10 g with [[starch]] at least 1.9 g, [[fat]]s at least 2 g.

==Uses==
Dried tiger nut has a smooth, tender, sweet, and nutty taste. It can be consumed raw, roasted, dried, baked or as [[Horchata|tiger nut milk]], [[tiger nut drink]] or oil.

[[File:Horchata Chufas from Alboraya for sale in Valencia, Spain.jpg|thumb|Bulk Horchata Chufas from Alboraya for sale in neighboring Valencia, Spain.]]

===Drink===
In Spain, the drink now known as horchata de chufa (also sometimes called horchata de chufas or, in West African countries such as Nigeria and Mali, ''kunun aya'') is the original form of horchata.{{dubious|date=May 2020|horchata was originally a ''barley'' drink, as seen from its etymology}} It is made from soaked, ground and sweetened tiger nuts mixed with sugar and water.<ref name="soto">{{cite journal|last1=Roselló-Soto|first1=Elena|last2=Poojary|first2=Mahesha M.|last3=Barba|first3=Francisco J.|last4=Koubaa|first4=Mohamed|last5=Lorenzo|first5=Jose M.|last6=Mañes|first6=Jordi|last7=Moltó|first7=Juan Carlos|year=2018|title=Thermal and non-thermal preservation techniques of tiger nuts' beverage "horchata de chufa". Implications for food safety, nutritional and quality properties|journal=Food Research International|volume=105|pages=945–951|doi=10.1016/j.foodres.2017.12.014|issn=0963-9969|pmid=29433293}}</ref>
It remains popular in Spain, where a regulating council exists to ensure the quality and traceability of the product in relation to the designation of origin. There it is served ice-cold as a natural refreshment in the summer, often served with [[fartons]].
The majority of the Spanish tiger nut crop is utilised in the production of horchata de chufa. [[Alboraya]] is the most important production centre.

The tubers can be roasted and ground into a [[coffee substitute]].<ref>{{Cite book|last=Angier|first=Bradford|url=https://archive.org/details/fieldguidetoedib00angi/page/58/mode/2up|title=Field Guide to Edible Wild Plants|publisher=Stackpole Books|year=1974|isbn=0-8117-0616-8|location=Harrisburg, PA|page=58|oclc=799792|author-link=Bradford Angier}}</ref>

===Food===

[[File:Cyperus esculentus MS 4388.jpg|thumb|right|Dried tubers sold at the market of [[Banfora]], [[Burkina Faso]].]]

The tubers are [[Eating|edible]] raw or cooked.<ref name=":2">{{Cite book|last1=Elias|first1=Thomas S.|title=Edible Wild Plants: A North American Field Guide to Over 200 Natural Foods|last2=Dykeman|first2=Peter A.|publisher=[[Sterling Publishing|Sterling]]|year=2009|isbn=978-1-4027-6715-9|location=New York|page=130|oclc=244766414|orig-date=1982}}</ref> They have a slightly sweet, nutty flavour, compared to the more bitter-tasting tuber of the related ''[[Cyperus rotundus]]'' (purple nutsedge). They are quite hard and are generally soaked in water before they can be eaten, making them much softer and giving them a better texture. They are a popular snack in West Africa. The tubers can also be dried and ground into flour.<ref name=":2" />

In [[Northern Nigeria]], it is called ''aya'' and it is usually eaten fresh. It is sometimes dried and later rehydrated and eaten. A snack made by toasting the nuts and sugar coating it is popular among the [[Hausa people|Hausa]] children of [[Northern Nigeria]]. Also, a drink known as ''kunun aya'' is made by processing the nuts with [[Date (fruit)|dates]] and later sieved and served chilled.

In Egypt, tiger nuts are known by the name ''ḥab el ʿAzīz'' and after softening it by soaking in water, it is sold on hand carts as a street food.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Hab' el Aziz |url=https://www.fondazioneslowfood.com/en/ark-of-taste-slow-food/hab-el-aziz/}}</ref> Its popularity was depicted in movies, such as the song named after it, "Ḥab el ʿAzīz".

Flour of roasted tiger nut is sometimes added to biscuits and other bakery products as well as in making oil, soap, and starch extracts. It is also used for the production of nougat, jam, beer, and as a flavoring agent in ice cream and in the preparation of [[kunu]] (a local beverage in Nigeria).{{Citation needed|date=December 2019|reason=removed citation to predatory publisher content}}  Kunu is a nonalcoholic beverage prepared mainly from cereals (such as millet or sorghum) by heating and mixing with spices (dandelion, alligator pepper, ginger, licorice) and sugar. To make up for the poor nutritional value of kunu prepared from cereals, tiger nut was found to be a good substitute for cereal grains. Tiger nut oil can be used naturally with salads or for deep frying. It is considered to be a high-quality oil. Tiger nut "milk" has been tried as an alternative source of milk in fermented products, such as yogurt production, and other fermented products common in some African countries and can thus be useful replacing [[milk]] in the diet of people intolerant to [[lactose]] to a certain extent.<ref name=tiger />

===Oil===
Since the tubers of ''C. esculentus'' contain 20-36% oil, it has been suggested as potential oil crop for the production of [[biodiesel]].<ref name=zhang/> One study found that chufa produced 1.5 metric tonnes of oil per hectare (174 gallons/acre) based on a tuber yield of 5.67 t/ha and an oil content of 26.4%.<ref name="sedge">{{cite journal | last1=Makareviciene | first1=Violeta | last2=Gumbyte | first2=Milda | last3=Yunik | first3=Anatolii | last4=Kalenska | first4=Svitlana | last5=Kalenskii | first5=Viktor | last6=Rachmetov | first6=Dzhamal | last7=Sendzikiene | first7=Egle | title=Opportunities for the use of chufa sedge in biodiesel production | journal=Industrial Crops and Products | volume=50 | year=2013 | issn=0926-6690 | doi=10.1016/j.indcrop.2013.08.036 | pages=633–637}}</ref> A similar 6-year study found tuber yields ranging from 4.02 to 6.75 t/ha, with an average oil content of 26.5% and an average oil yield of 1.47 t/ha.<ref>Bilali et al., "Exploring Serbian consumers' attitude toward ethical values of organic, fair-trade and typical/traditional products" The Fifth International Scientific Conference, Rural Development 2011, Proceedings, Volume 5, Book 1, p. 337.</ref> The oil of the tuber was found to contain 18% saturated ([[palmitic acid]] and [[stearic acid]]) and 82% unsaturated ([[oleic acid]] and [[linoleic acid]]) [[fatty acid]]s.<ref name=zhang>{{cite journal|title= Yellow nut-sedge tuber oil as a fuel |doi=10.1016/0926-6690(96)89446-5 | volume=5 |issue= 3|journal=Industrial Crops and Products |pages=177–181|year= 1996|last1= Zhang|first1= He Yuan|last2= Hanna|first2= Milford A|last3= Ali|first3= Yusuf|last4= Nan|first4= Lu}}</ref>

===Fishing bait===
The boiled nuts are used in the UK as a bait for [[Common carp|carp]]. The nuts have to be prepared in a prescribed manner to prevent harm to the fish. The nuts are soaked in water for 24 hours, and then boiled for 20 minutes or longer until fully expanded. Some anglers then leave the boiled nuts to ferment for 24–48 hours, which can enhance their effectiveness. If the nuts are not properly prepared, they can be toxic to carp. This was originally thought to have been the cause of death of [[Benson (fish)|Benson]], a large, well-known female carp weighing {{Convert|54|lb|kg|abbr=on}} found floating dead in a fishing lake, with a bag of unprepared tiger nuts lying nearby, empty, on the bank. An examination of the fish by a [[taxidermist]] concluded tiger nut poisoning was not the cause of death, but rather the fish had died naturally.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Bailey |first=John |url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB125051804649836945 |title=The extraordinary life and suspicious death of Benson the giant carp |work=The Guardian |date=5 August 2009 |access-date=21 March 2019 |archive-date=18 October 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091018071147/http://online.wsj.com/article/SB125051804649836945.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

=== History ===
It has been suggested that the extinct [[hominin]] ''[[Paranthropus boisei]]'' (the "Nutcracker Man") subsisted on tiger nuts.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Macho |first=Gabriele A. |date=2014-01-08 |title=Baboon Feeding Ecology Informs the Dietary Niche of Paranthropus boisei |journal=PLOS ONE |volume=9 |issue=1 |article-number=e84942 |bibcode=2014PLoSO...984942M |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0084942 |issn=1932-6203 |pmc=3885648 |pmid=24416315 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

''Cyperus esculentus'' was one of the oldest cultivated plants in prehistoric and [[Ancient Egypt]], where it was an important food. Roots of wild chufa have been found at [[Wadi Kubbaniya]], north of [[Aswan]], dating to around 16,000 BC.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Sanderson |first1=Helen |title=The Cultural History of Plants |date=2005 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=0-415-92746-3 |editor1-last=Prance |editor1-first=Ghillean |page=74 |editor2-last=Nesbitt |editor2-first=Mark}}</ref> Dry tubers also appear later in tombs of the [[Predynastic Egypt|Predynastic period]], around 3000 BC. During that time, ''C. esculentus'' tubers were consumed either boiled in beer, roasted, or as sweets made of ground tubers with honey.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Moshe |first1=N |year=1992 |title=A Sweetmeat Plant, a Perfume Plant and their Weedy Relatives: A Chapter in the History of C. Esculentus L. and C. Rotundus L. |journal=Economic Botany |volume=46 |pages=64–71 |doi=10.1007/bf02985255 |s2cid=37815353}}</ref> The tubers were also used medicinally, taken orally, as an ointment, or as an enema, and used in fumigants to sweeten the smell of homes or clothing.<ref name="god">{{cite journal |last1=Defelice |first1=MS |year=2002 |title=Yellow Nutsedge: ''Cyperus esculentus'' L. — Snack Food of the Gods1 |journal=Weed Technology |volume=16 |issue=4 |pages=901–7 |doi=10.1614/0890-037x(2002)016[0901:yncels]2.0.co;2|s2cid=85720525 }}</ref> Chufa continued to be an important source of food in the [[Dynastic Egypt|Dynastic period]], and cultivation of the plant remained exclusively in Egypt.<ref>Daniel Zohary and Maria Hopf, ''Domestication of plants in the Old World'', third edition (Oxford: University Press, 2000), p. 198</ref> The tomb of the [[vizier]] [[Rekhmire]] from the 15th century BCE, shows peasants preparing and measuring tiger nuts to make votive cakes as offerings to the god [[Amun]].<ref>{{Cite news |title=Loathed By Farmers, Loved By Ancients: The Strange History Of Tiger Nuts |work=NPR |url=https://www.npr.org/sections/thesalt/2016/04/27/472581773/loathed-by-farmers-loved-by-ancients-the-strange-history-of-tiger-nuts}}</ref><ref>{{Cite episode |title=Ancient Egyptian Tiger Nut Cake |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=D_FabMorrMU |access-date=25 January 2022 |series=Tasting History with Max Miller |series-link=Tasting History with Max Miller |first=Max |last=Miller |network=[[YouTube]] |date=31 August 2021 |season= |series-no= |number= |minutes= |time= |transcript= |transcript-url= |quote= |language=}}</ref> The modern name for tiger nuts in Egypt is حب العزيز ''(ḥab el ʿAzīz = grains of [[Al-Aziz Billah|Al-Aziz]]'') named after the Fatimid ruler who was reputedly fond of it.<ref name=":1" />
